blocks.text: What Lazur does in Slack on Mac

Slack gets busy fast. Threads run long, channels pile up, and the answer you need sits somewhere higher up the screen. Lazur sits in the notch at the top of your Mac display. Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask your question, and it looks at the Slack window you have open.

You do not copy the thread into a chat window first. Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When you let go, it stops looking. It answers out loud, draws a circle and a label around anything you ask it to find, and guides you one step at a time when you ask how to do something.

Lazur does four jobs in Slack. It explains what is on screen, points at things, guides you through a feature, and drafts or dictates text at your cursor. The sections below take each job in turn, using the Slack tasks that Slack's own help pages cover.
Which Slack tasks an AI assistant handles well

Most Slack work falls into a few groups. You catch up on messages, answer people, find a setting, or get words into a message quickly. Lazur helps with the first three by reading and explaining. It helps with the last one by drafting and dictating.

Slack's quick start guide names the sidebar, Home, DMs, Activity, Files, the message field, search, the Create button and the profile menu as the first things new users need. Those are the places where most questions start. Use those names when you ask Lazur where something is.

A note on the research. Slack does not publish which help articles get the most views, so this list is not based on search volume. It is based on the Mac help topics Slack publishes. Those topics cover shortcuts, the Enter key, updates and message history. They show where Slack expects people to need help.

items: Catch up: “what did I miss in this channel?”
Reply: “draft a reply, Thursday works, keep it short”
Find a setting: “where is the Enter key setting?”
Type by voice: click the compose box, then hold fn and talk.
Check for updates: “walk me through checking for updates”

blocks.text: Ask about a thread on screen with ⌥ ⌘

This is the move you will use most. Open the thread, scroll to the messages that matter, then hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask. Lazur answers out loud when you let go. Ask a follow-up while the same window stays open, because the screen is what Lazur reads.

items: Open the channel or thread in the Slack Mac app.
Scroll until the part you care about is on screen. Lazur reads only what is visible.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, for example, “sum up this thread, what do they need from me?”
Release the keys and listen to the answer. Ask a follow-up if you need more.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. A long thread in a launch channel has many replies, and your name appears in the middle of it. You hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what the thread needs from you. Lazur reads the messages on screen and says what is still open. If the answer skips a point, scroll up and ask again.
Three edge cases catch people out.

items: Collapsed replies: expand the thread first, so the messages are visible on screen.
Old messages: Lazur cannot read messages you have not loaded. Scroll to them first.
Whole workspace: Lazur does not search all of Slack for you. Use search, then ask about the result on screen.

blocks.text: Search is a different job. Use ⌘ + G to search the workspace, or ⌘ + F to search the conversation you are in. For the full steps, see [how to search messages in Slack on Mac](/how-to/search-messages-in-slack).
Draft a reply at your cursor, then read it before you send

Drafting follows the same pattern, with one extra step. Click into the reply box or the thread reply field first. That sets your cursor. Then hold ⌥ ⌘, say what you want to say, and let go. Lazur types the draft at the cursor.

Worked example. Sam asks in a thread whether Thursday works for the review. You want to say yes and ask about the budget. You click the thread reply box, hold ⌥ ⌘, and say, “draft a reply, yes to Thursday, ask about the budget.” Lazur types the draft at your cursor. You change one word, check the date, and press Enter.
Short, specific asks give better drafts. Give the facts, the tone and the length. A simple shape works well: the answer, one detail, and one question back. These asks show the pattern.

items: “Draft a reply. Yes to Thursday, ask about the budget.”
“Draft a short thanks. No emojis, one line.”
“Draft a polite no. Suggest next week instead.”

blocks.text: Read every draft before you send. Lazur types the words, but it does not press Enter. It does not send messages for you. A draft can read well on screen and still carry the wrong date or name, so check both every time. Only 7% of desk workers consider AI outputs completely trustworthy for work, according to Slack's survey. The check is worth doing.
Dictate Slack messages on a Mac with fn

Dictation is the fastest way to write a longer update. Click the message box first. Then hold fn, say the update the way you would say it in standup, and let go. Lazur types clean text at your cursor. Filler words drop out, and text you speak as a list can come out formatted as one.

items: Click the message box in the channel or thread you want to post in.
Hold fn and speak in full sentences. Name each point in the order you want it read.
Let go of fn. Read the text in the box before you send it.
Send with Return or ⌘ + Enter, depending on your Enter key setting.

blocks.text: Dictation writes what you said, cleaned up. It does not decide what to say. Add names, product words and short phrases to your personal dictionary so they come out right. Lazur also keeps snippets and clipboard slots for text you reuse. Dictation is unlimited on both Lazur plans.
Speaking is often quicker than typing for a status update. To compare your own speed, try the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test). Then decide which way suits your standup.

Common mistake: holding fn with no field focused. The text then has nowhere useful to land. Click first, then hold. Also check that the right thread is open, because the text goes to whatever field has your cursor.
Set the Enter key so dictation does not send early
Slack's Enter key setting decides what Return does. Under one option, Return sends the message. If you dictate several lines and the message goes out early, this setting is the likely cause.
Open Preferences with ⌘ + , and go to Advanced. Choose the option that fits how you write.

blocks.caption: From Slack's Enter key preference article

blocks.text: Pick “Start a new line” if you often dictate several lines. Breaks then stay in the box until you press ⌘ + Enter. The trade-off is one extra key press each time you send.
If messages still send early, check this setting before you blame dictation.
Slack keyboard shortcuts on Mac worth learning

Shortcuts are faster than asking for basic moves. Learn the few you use daily, and ask Lazur when you forget one. The table below comes from Slack's keyboard shortcuts article, plus the navigation article for ⌘ + K.

rows: Open the quick switcher for channels, DMs and people
Jump to the most recent unread message
Expand or collapse the workspace switcher
blocks.caption: From Slack's keyboard shortcuts and navigation help pages

blocks.title: Check two shortcuts in the app
blocks.text: Slack's shortcuts page lists Activity as ⌘ + ⇧ + M, but its navigation page lists Ctrl + 3. Slack also says custom shortcuts are not currently possible, so you cannot fix a clash yourself. Test the key in the app before you rely on it.
Start with ⌘ + K. It opens the quick switcher, where you type a channel, DM or person name and jump there. It is the simplest way to leave a thread and reach another one.

For the full shortcut list inside Slack, see [how to show keyboard shortcuts in Slack on Mac](/how-to/show-the-keyboard-shortcuts-list-in-slack). For unread messages, see [how to jump to unread messages in Slack on Mac](/how-to/jump-to-the-latest-unread-message-in-slack).
Check your macOS and Slack versions before you start

Lazur runs on your Mac, and Slack sets its own version rules. Slack's system requirements page lists macOS 13 or later and Slack desktop app 4.44 or later. Slack updates those requirements twice per year, in May and November, so check them again when you update.

Check your Mac version under Apple menu > About This Mac. For Slack, use Slack > Check for Updates to pick up the latest build. Slack's release notes list version 4.53.280 from November 3, 2026, with a note that it contains security improvements and an update is recommended, so keeping current matters.

items: Direct download: choose Slack > Check for Updates, then click Restart to Apply Update.
Mac App Store: open the App Store and check the Updates section.
Either way: Slack installs to /Applications and updates on its own when a new version is released.

blocks.text: Mind the support dates. Slack ends support for macOS 13 and below on November 9, 2026. If your Mac runs that system or an older one, plan the upgrade before that date, not after your team notices the problem.
Free plan message history and what an AI assistant can see

Slack's free plan keeps messages and files searchable for 90 days. Messages and files more than one year old are permanently deleted, according to Slack's message limits article. Old content can disappear from Slack itself, not only from your view.

Lazur works with what Slack shows you. It cannot bring back content Slack no longer keeps. If you need a decision from last year, look for it in a pinned message or a document first. To keep key messages easy to find, see [how to pin a message in Slack on Mac](/how-to/pin-a-message-in-slack).

Slack's pricing page talks about access to the previous 12 months on paid plans, but its wording on that point is unclear. Check the pricing page before you plan around older history. Do not assume a paid plan keeps everything.
What Slack's Workforce Index says about AI and burnout

Slack's Workforce Index helps explain why quick answers matter to people who work in Slack all day. The June 2024 survey covered 10,045 workers in six countries, with fieldwork from March 6 to 22, 2024. Slack commissioned the survey, so treat these numbers as Slack's own research, not an independent study.

Three results stand out. 75% of knowledge workers use more apps than five years ago, and 67% expect that number to keep growing. Burnout is common, with 64% of desk workers reporting it once a month or more. Trust in AI output is low, with only 7% calling it completely trustworthy for work tasks.

What this means for you: a quick summary saves time only when you can trust it. Use Lazur to find the part of a thread worth reading, then read that part yourself before you reply to anything that matters.
Mistakes people make with an AI assistant in Slack

items: Asking about messages that are not on screen. Scroll first, then hold ⌥ ⌘.
Trusting a draft without reading it. Lazur types the words, but you choose to send.
Dictating with no field focused. Click the compose box before you hold fn.
Forgetting the Enter key setting. Dictated lines can send early when Return sends.
Asking for a summary of a whole channel with no limit. Ask a narrower question, such as “what changed since Monday?”
Expecting Lazur to act inside Slack. It does not click buttons or change settings. It points and guides you.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from a skipped step. Scroll, click and read first. Then ask. The habit is small, and it prevents most of these errors.
What to do next

items: Check that your Mac runs macOS 13 or later and that Slack is at 4.44 or later.
Set your Enter key option under Preferences > Advanced, as described above.
Download Lazur from the [download page](/download). The trial needs no credit card.
Test the asks in the list above on a thread you already know, so you can judge the answers.
Compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing) before you commit.

blocks.text: Privacy works like this. Lazur looks at the screen and listens only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Does Lazur work in the Slack Mac app?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur reads what is on your screen, so it works with the Slack Mac app and with Slack open in a browser tab. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask a question, and hold fn to dictate into the compose box.

faq.question: Is Lazur a Slack app or integration?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin, add-in or integration for Slack or any other app. Nothing is installed in your workspace. Lazur runs on your Mac and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

faq.question: Can Lazur send messages for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur writes the draft at your cursor. You read it and press Enter yourself. Lazur does not click buttons, so it never sends a message for you.

faq.question: Which keys do I hold?
faq.answer: Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app.

faq.question: Which Slack and macOS versions do I need?
faq.answer: Slack's system requirements page lists macOS 13 or later and Slack desktop app 4.44 or later. Slack revises these in May and November, so check the page when you install or update.

faq.question: Does Lazur see my whole Slack history?
faq.answer: No. Lazur sees the messages on your screen while you hold the shortcut. Scroll to older messages so they load on screen, then ask again.

faq.question: What does it cost?
faq.answer: Lazur has a free trial that needs no credit card. Plan prices are on the pricing page, so check them there before you pay.

faq.question: Is my audio or screen stored?
faq.answer: Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Does dictation work in Slack on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Click the compose box, hold fn, speak, and let go. Read the text before you send it, and check your Enter key setting so a line break does not send early.
